topics.title: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
topics.html:
1. DNS: domain → IP (browser cache → OS → recursive resolver → authoritative NS).
  2. TCP handshake (SYN→SYN-ACK→ACK). HTTPS: TLS handshake on top.
  3. HTTP GET. Server returns HTML.
  4. Parse HTML → DOM. Parse CSS → CSSOM. Together → Render Tree.
  5. Layout (reflow): compute geometry. Paint: fill pixels. Composite: GPU merges layers.
  6. CSS is render-blocking. JS without async/defer is parser-blocking.
Reflow vs repaint vs compositing?
Reflow: geometry recalculation, most expensive. Repaint: pixel update without geometry change. Compositing: GPU-only, cheapest. transform/opacity only trigger compositing — 60fps even on weak devices.
💬 Say it like this

I go through it in steps: DNS to find the IP, the TCP and TLS handshake, then the HTTP request. The server returns HTML, the browser parses it into the DOM and the CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into the render tree, then does layout, paint and composite.

The part that matters for my work is what blocks it. CSS blocks rendering, and a script without async or defer blocks parsing — that is usually where a slow first paint comes from.

topics.title: DOM event propagation. Event delegation.
topics.html:
Events travel three phases: Capturing (window down to target), Target, Bubbling (rises back to window).

el.addEventListener("click", handler)           // bubbling (default)
el.addEventListener("click", handler, true)     // capturing
el.addEventListener("click", handler, { capture:true, once:true, passive:true })
// stopPropagation() — stops event moving to next element.
// stopImmediatePropagation() — stops propagation AND other handlers on same element.
// preventDefault() — cancels browser default — does NOT stop propagation.
// Event delegation — one listener on parent, not N on N children
document.querySelector("#list")!.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const li = (e.target as Element).closest("li[data-id]");
  if (!li) return;
  handleSelect((li as HTMLElement).dataset.id!);
});
💬 Say it like this

DOM events have three phases. First capturing — from window down to the target. Then the target phase. Then bubbling — back up to window. By default, listeners fire in the bubbling phase. Event delegation is one listener on a parent instead of one on each child — works because clicks on children bubble up. React's synthetic event system works the same way internally.

What does passive: true do?
Tells browser handler will never call preventDefault() — browser starts scrolling immediately without waiting for JS. Critical for scroll/touch performance.

topics.title: XSS and CSRF — explain and defend.
topics.html:
• XSS: attacker injects malicious JS. React auto-escapes JSX. Hole: dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Fix: DOMPurify + Content-Security-Policy header.
  • CSRF: forces user's browser to send authenticated request. Fix: CSRF tokens, SameSite=Strict cookies, check Origin header.
localStorage / sessionStorage / cookies / IndexedDB?
localStorage: ~5MB, persists forever, sync. sessionStorage: cleared on tab close. cookies: ~4KB, sent with every HTTP request — HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite for session cookies. IndexedDB: large async transactional store for offline/PWA. Never store auth tokens in localStorage — XSS-readable. HttpOnly cookies are safer.
💬 Say it like this

XSS is when someone manages to run their JavaScript on my page. React escapes everything in JSX by default, so the usual hole is dangerouslySetInnerHTML — if I need HTML from the server, I sanitise it with DOMPurify and add a Content-Security-Policy.

CSRF is different: the attacker makes the user's browser send a real request with their cookies. The defence is on the cookie and the server side — SameSite cookies, a CSRF token and an origin check. And I never keep access tokens in localStorage, because any XSS can read them; an HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript.

topics.title: React events vs native JS events — what's different?
topics.html:
• Event pooling & normalization: React wraps native events in a cross-browser synthetic event object. Synthetic events are reused (pooled) for performance — you can't access them asynchronously (e.g., in an async handler). If you need async access, call e.persist().
  • Event delegation: React attaches all listeners to the root container, not to each element. All events bubble up through React's own system. Saves memory and improves performance on large lists.
  • Capture phase: Native DOM events have 3 phases (capture → target → bubbling). React's synthetic system doesn't expose capture phase by default. Use onClickCapture (with "Capture" suffix) to catch in capture phase.
  • Stopping propagation: e.stopPropagation() in React only stops React's synthetic bubbling, NOT native DOM bubbling. If a native listener is attached to the same element outside React, it still fires. Use e.nativeEvent.stopImmediatePropagation() to stop all listeners.
  • Passive listeners: Native addEventListener(..., {passive: true}) tells browser "I promise not to call preventDefault()" — lets browser scroll immediately. React event handlers are NOT passive by default, which can hurt scroll performance. This is a common gotcha.
  • Return false does nothing: Unlike vanilla JS, React's return false from an event handler doesn't prevent default. You must call e.preventDefault() explicitly.
// Native DOM (3 listeners, capture → target → bubble)
element.addEventListener('click', handleCapture, true);
element.addEventListener('click', handleTarget);
element.addEventListener('click', handleBubble);

// React (all delegated to root, synthetic system)
<div onClickCapture={handleCapture} onClick={handleBubble} />

// Async access requires e.persist() (React 16)
function Form() {
  const handleChange = (e) => {
    e.persist(); // Or e.target is null after async
    setTimeout(() => console.log(e.target.value), 0);
  };
  return <input onChange={handleChange} />;
}

// Stop React bubbling only — native listener still fires
<div onClick={(e) => {
  e.stopPropagation(); // Stops React bubbling
  // But native listeners on same element still receive event
}}>
💬 Say it like this

React uses synthetic events for performance and cross-browser consistency. All listeners are delegated to the root element, not attached individually. This saves memory and allows React to optimize. The synthetic event object is pooled — reused after the handler runs — so you can't access it asynchronously without e.persist(). One key difference: React's stopPropagation() only stops React bubbling, not native DOM bubbling. And React event handlers aren't passive by default, which can block scrolling during handlers that call preventDefault(). Also, onClickCapture with Capture suffix catches in the capture phase.

Why pool events if modern JS has GC?
Memory churn. High-frequency events (scroll, mousemove) create event objects constantly. Even with fast GC, allocation pressure matters. Pooling reuses the same object. React 17+ relaxed pooling, but synthetic events still exist.
Can I mix React and native listeners on the same element?
Yes, but order is unpredictable because React listeners are on root, native on element. React listeners fire after capture, native listeners in their order. Avoid mixing if possible.
Why no passive listeners in React by default?
React can't guarantee handlers won't call preventDefault(). Setting passive would error if code calls it. Trade-off: scroll performance vs developer freedom. Consider <div onTouchMove={handler} onWheel={handler}> carefully in mobile.

topics.title: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter — full browser and rendering pipeline.
topics.html:
• 1. DNS lookup: Browser queries DNS server (recursive resolvers → root nameserver → TLD → authoritative). OS caches, browser caches, ISP caches to avoid multiple lookups. ~50-300ms typical.
  • 2. TCP handshake (3-way): SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Establishes connection. ~30-100ms per RTT (round-trip time).
  • 3. TLS/SSL handshake (if HTTPS): ClientHello → ServerHello + cert + DH params → ClientKeyExchange → ChangeCipherSpec. Adds another RTT or two. Total ~100-300ms for DNS + TCP + TLS combined.
  • 4. HTTP request sent: GET / with Host header, User-Agent, Accept, etc. Single TCP packet usually.
  • 5. Server processes request: Routing, middleware, database queries, template rendering. Server sends response with status, headers, HTML body.
  • 6. HTML received incrementally (streaming): Browser doesn't wait for full HTML. It processes as data arrives (chunked transfer encoding). Parser builds DOM tree on-the-fly.
  • 7. HTML parsing & DOM construction: Tokenizer breaks HTML into tokens. Parser builds DOM nodes. If it encounters <script> or <link rel="stylesheet">, it stops and fetches/executes (render-blocking). With async, script loads in background. With defer, script waits until DOM is ready.
  • 8. CSS parsing & CSSOM construction: CSS is render-blocking (full CSSOM required before first render). External stylesheets block rendering until fetched and parsed.
  • 9. Render tree construction (DOM + CSSOM): Browser combines DOM and CSSOM. Skips invisible nodes (display: none). Creates render tree.
  • 10. Layout (reflow): Browser calculates exact pixel positions and sizes for each element. Considers viewport size, box-model, flexbox/grid algorithms. Single-threaded, expensive. Triggered by: DOM changes, CSS changes, offsetHeight, scrollTop reads, window resize.
  • 11. Paint (rasterization): Browser converts layout into pixels. Creates paint records. Multiple paint layers possible (GPU-accelerated with will-change, transform, opacity).
  • 12. Composite: Browser combines all paint layers in correct z-order, sends to GPU, displays on screen. 60fps = 16.67ms per frame budget.
  • 13. JavaScript execution: Happens on main thread. Blocks layout, paint, composite if it runs long. <script> tags (non-async, non-defer) block HTML parsing. Long JS tasks cause jank (dropped frames).
  • 14. Resource loading continues: Images, fonts, other assets load asynchronously. Don't block rendering but do trigger layout/paint when they load (unless width/height attributes present).

Critical resource order for fast page load:

  1. Preconnect DNS + TCP + TLS for critical 3rd-party domains: <link rel="preconnect" href="...">
  2. Critical CSS inline in <head> or small external file (blocks render)
  3. HTML content
  4. Non-critical JS with async or defer
  5. Fonts with font-display: swap (display fallback, swap when ready)
  6. Images lazy-loaded or with width/height to avoid layout shift
// Bad: blocks HTML parsing
<script src="heavy.js"></script>

// Good: loads in parallel, executes after DOM ready
<script src="heavy.js" defer></script>

// Okay: loads in parallel, executes ASAP (may before DOM ready)
<script src="small.js" async></script>

// Preload critical fonts early
<link rel="preload" href="font.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

// Prevent layout shift from images
<img src="..." width="800" height="600" alt="" />

// CSS blocks rendering — keep it critical only
<style>body { margin: 0; }</style>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="critical.css">
💬 Say it like this

When you press Enter, the browser first does a DNS lookup to resolve the domain to an IP. Then it opens a TCP connection and negotiates TLS if HTTPS. Once connected, it sends an HTTP GET request. The server responds with HTML, which the browser starts parsing immediately — not waiting for the full response. During parsing, if it hits a <script> tag without async/defer, parsing stops until the script runs. CSS is also render-blocking — the browser waits for the full CSSOM before rendering anything. Once HTML and CSS are both ready, the browser builds a render tree, calculates layout (which is expensive), then paints pixels and composites the result onto the screen. JavaScript runs on the main thread, so any long-running code blocks layout and paint, causing jank. Images load asynchronously and don't block the first render, but if you don't specify width/height, they can cause layout shift when they load. The key optimization: get critical CSS into the <head> early, defer non-critical scripts, preconnect to important third-party domains, and make sure images have dimensions.

What's the difference between layout and paint?
Layout is calculating positions and sizes (expensive, single-threaded). Paint is rasterizing those boxes into pixels. Both happen on main thread. Composite (combining layers) can happen on GPU. Changing transform or opacity doesn't trigger layout or paint — only composite — so those are fast.
Why is CSS render-blocking?
Browser can't render until it knows all styles. If it rendered before CSS arrived, there'd be visible flash of unstyled content. So it waits for CSSOM. Exception: media queries — browser can render blocks not matching current media queries, but safety-first is to wait.
What's the difference between async and defer?
async: download in parallel, run as soon as ready (may interrupt HTML parsing). defer: download in parallel, run after HTML fully parsed, in order. For independent scripts: async. For order-dependent: defer. No attribute: blocks parsing.
Why do font loads cause layout shift?
If you don't declare font-display: swap, browser waits for the font file before displaying text. Meanwhile, fallback font is wider/taller. When web font loads, text reflows — layout shift. Use font-display: swap or ensure web font and fallback have similar metrics with @font-face size-adjust.
How long does each step take?
DNS: 50-300ms. TCP: 30-100ms per RTT. TLS: another 100-300ms (1-2 RTTs). Server processing: depends. HTML parsing: concurrent with download. CSS parsing: 10-50ms. Layout: 10-100ms depending on DOM size. Paint: similar. Composite: <1ms if GPU-accelerated. Network dominates for most sites.

topics.title: The browser rendering pipeline — from parsing to the frame on screen.
topics.html:
HTML text → Parse → DOM tree CSS text → Parse → CSSOM DOM + CSSOM → Style → Render Tree (visual nodes + ComputedStyle) → Layout → boxes, positions and sizes (also called Reflow) → Paint → draw instructions, in the correct order (z-index) → Raster → pixels / textures for each layer → Composite → layers put together into a FRAME → screen
  • Parse. The HTML parser turns the text into the DOM tree. Stylesheets are parsed into the CSSOM, a structure built for fast lookup of selectors. Both happen as tasks on the main thread.
  • Style (in DevTools: Recalculate Style). The browser walks the DOM, finds the visual elements and builds the Render Tree. Each node points to a DOM node and to its ComputedStyle — the final list of declarations after specificity is resolved. <head>, <script> and anything with display: none are not in this tree; visibility: hidden is, because it still takes space.
  • Layout. The render tree knows the styles but no geometry yet. Layout walks the tree and gives every node a box with exact coordinates and size, calculated recursively from the children up. It is expensive, so the browser caches a lot of it.
  • Paint. The browser records the drawing instructions for each node in the right order — z-index, scroll containers, overlapping elements. Chromium uses the Skia graphics library for this.
  • Raster and composite. The instructions are turned into real pixels, usually per layer and per tile, and the GPU puts the layers together into one frame that is sent to the display.

Which threads are involved:

  • Main thread — parsing, style, layout, paint recording, and all your JavaScript. This is the one you can block, and if you block it nothing is rendered.
  • Compositor thread — puts layers together, handles scrolling and transform/opacity animations. It can keep scrolling smooth even while the main thread is busy.
  • Raster threads — turn paint instructions into bitmaps for the tiles.
  • GPU process — uploads the textures and draws the final frame.
  • Network and worker threads — downloads, and your own Web Workers, which run JavaScript off the main thread.
Why this matters in practice: not every change costs the same. Changing width, top or font-size → layout + paint + composite. Changing background-color → paint + composite. Changing transform or opacity → composite only, and it can run on the compositor thread, which is why animations should use them. Reading offsetHeight right after a style change forces a synchronous layout — do that in a loop and you get layout thrashing. With 60 frames per second, one frame is about 16 ms for everything.
💬 Say it like this

The browser gets HTML text and parses it into the DOM tree. The CSS is parsed into the CSSOM. Then in the style step it combines them into the render tree, which contains only the elements that are actually visible, each one with its computed style. Elements in the head, scripts and anything with display: none are not there.

After that comes layout, where every node gets a real box with coordinates and size. Then paint, where the browser records the drawing instructions in the correct order, and finally raster and composite, where the layers become pixels and the GPU puts them together into one frame that goes to the screen.

The important part for me as a developer is that the steps have different costs. Changing width or position runs layout, paint and composite. Changing background colour skips layout. Changing transform or opacity is composite only and can run on the compositor thread, so animations stay smooth even if the main thread is busy. And the main thread does parsing, style, layout, paint recording and all my JavaScript, so a long task there blocks the whole frame.

What is layout thrashing?
Writing a style and then immediately reading a layout value like offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect. The read forces the browser to run layout synchronously, and in a loop it runs on every iteration. The fix is to batch all reads first, then all writes.
What creates a new compositor layer?
Things like transform animations, will-change, position: fixed, video and canvas. Layers make animation cheap, but each one costs memory, so promoting everything makes performance worse.
When does the pipeline actually run?
The browser runs it as part of the event loop, before the next frame is painted, so requestAnimationFrame callbacks run just before style and layout. If a task is longer than the frame budget, the frame is late and the user sees jank.
